## Abstract

There is no comprehensive synthesis of supportive care interventions for patients with hematologic malignancies receiving transplantation and cellular therapies (TCTs). This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to characterize randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of TCT supportive care interventions and examine effects on patient-reported outcomes (PROs). We systematically searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycInfo, Web of Science, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0. Findings were grouped by intervention and PRO type and synthesized narratively, with exploratory random-effects meta-analyses estimating pooled intervention effects on anxiety, depression, and quality of life (QOL). Fifty-three RCTs (1992-2025) met inclusion criteria. The search yielded only RCTs of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) recipients, although we included all transplantation and cellular therapies. Studies varied in sample size (11-711), participant demographics (mean age, 33-63 years; 22%-64% women), and PROs. There were 9 intervention categories: cognitive behavioral (n = 5), exercise only (n = 17), expressive helping (n = 2), mind-body/stress management (n = 7), multimodal (exercise plus another modality; n = 6), music/art (n = 12), palliative care (n = 2), positive psychology (n = 1), and self-management/self-efficacy (n = 5). Interventions were mostly feasible and acceptable, with promising improvements in psychological distress, QOL, and physical outcomes. Meta-analysis showed nonsignificant trends toward exercise interventions improving QOL (standardized mean differences [SMD], 0.09) and music/art interventions reducing acute depressive symptoms (SMD, −0.26). Among patients undergoing HSCT for hematologic malignancies, supportive care interventions show feasibility, acceptability, and promise for improving PROs. However, larger, rigorously designed RCTs using standardized PRO measures are needed to establish efficacy.

## Introduction

Transplantation and cellular therapies (TCTs), including hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), offer a potential cure for hematologic malignancies but can cause significant toxicities.1, 2, 3, 4 Patients frequently experience treatment-related psychological (eg, anxiety, depression) and physical (eg, fatigue, pain) symptoms that negatively affect quality of life (QOL) throughout transplantation and recovery.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 Supportive care, which aims to prevent or treat treatment-related symptoms and provide physical, psychological, social, and spiritual support for patients and families,11 is uniquely positioned to address symptom burden across the TCT continuum, from pretreatment to post-TCT recovery and survivorship.12, 13, 14

Recognition of persistent unmet TCT psychosocial care needs and shortages in specialty mental health and palliative care clinicians has spurred the development of diverse supportive care interventions.12 Notably, these interventions increasingly focus on scalable delivery methods (eg, phone-based delivery by nonspecialty clinicians) and digital health technologies to improve access and dissemination and implementation in clinical settings.15 Existing supportive care interventions for this population vary in psychosocial and behavioral content, interventionist training and specialty, timing of delivery based on treatment phase, and target subpopulations.16, 17, 18

Although previous literature reviews describe supportive care interventions for TCT recipients, notable gaps remain.19 Existing systematic reviews are outdated (literature searches from 1959 to 2014)20 and focus on HSCT without including newer TCTs (eg, chimeric antigen receptor [CAR] T-cell therapy) that have been US Food and Drug Administration approved within the last 6 years.21, 22, 23 Moreover, synthesis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) testing intervention effects on patient-reported outcomes (PROs) is limited, thereby limiting our understanding of patient experiences, identification of risk factors for adverse health-related outcomes, and future intervention development.24

This systematic review and meta-analysis addresses these gaps by providing an updated synthesis of supportive care interventions for patients undergoing TCT, including novel therapies.25 Herein, we define supportive care interventions as non–disease-directed, primarily psychosocial or behavioral approaches in which TCT recipients actively apply skills intended to improve the physical, psychological, social, or spiritual well-being. We aimed to systematically review the literature on RCTs of TCT supportive care interventions and explore intervention effects on PROs via meta-analysis.24 We hypothesized that supportive care interventions would, overall, reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression and improve QOL. Ultimately, this rigorous synthesis has potential to enhance our understanding of the vast, heterogeneous, and multidisciplinary scope of supportive care interventions in TCT, guide the design of future interventions, and inform future research trials and clinical practice to improve psychosocial care for patients with hematologic malignancies undergoing TCT.

## Methods

### Overview

The systematic review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute manual for evidence synthesis.26 The protocol was registered in the international Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews database (identity: CRD42023462785).

### Search strategy

Keywords were linked to 3 main concepts: supportive care interventions, hematologic malignancies, and TCT. Search terms were compiled via the collaboration of a multidisciplinary group of clinicians and researchers in transplant oncology, psychiatry, and psychology, and library science (see supplemental Table 1 for search strategy). A senior reference librarian led searches of PubMed’s MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycInfo, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials databases, consistent with standard searches of biomedical databases, from database inception through August 2025.

### Eligibility criteria

We included supportive care intervention studies that (1) enrolled adults (aged ≥18 years) with hematologic malignancies undergoing TCT; (2) required patients to take an active role in applying psychosocial or behavioral skills; (3) were published in English; (4) used a quasi-experimental or RCT design with a usual care, wait-list, or attention-matched control group comparable in length with the intervention group; and (5) reported results of PROs.

We excluded studies that (1) enrolled children or adolescents (aged <18 years), patients without hematologic malignancies, or nonpatients (eg, caregivers); (2) involved nonsupportive care or passive interventions (eg, acupuncture); (3) were not published in English; (4) used non–quasi-experimental or RCT designs; (5) did not report PRO results (eg, reported only clinical [eg, lymphocyte count] or objective [eg, physical activity] outcomes); and/or (6) represented nonoriginal research (eg, commentaries) or conference abstracts (due to insufficient methodological detail for data extraction).

### Data extraction and quality assessment

Data from each study were extracted independently by 1 reviewer and verified by a second; discrepancies were resolved by consensus or a third reviewer. Two independent reviewers assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool.27 Risk of bias plots were generated using robvis (https://www.riskofbias.info/robvis).

### Statistical analysis

In addition to descriptive statistics, we conducted exploratory meta-analyses for psychosocial outcomes with sufficient data to generate pooled effect estimates. Psychosocial outcomes were defined as PROs of psychological or emotional well-being, social functioning or adjustment, or overall QOL. Trials were eligible for meta-analysis if they used validated, multi-item PRO measures of anxiety symptoms, depressive symptoms, and/or overall QOL. We prespecified that a minimum of 4 eligible studies testing a given type of intervention (eg, cognitive behavioral interventions) were required to perform pooled meta-analyses for each intervention type.28, 29, 30

All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.2) using the “meta” package. For continuous PROs, we analyzed change scores and expressed effects as mean differences (MDs) and standardized MDs (SMDs, Hedges g) using random-effects models with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using τ2 and I2. For continuous PROs, mean change scores and standard deviations (SDs) were extracted or derived for intervention and comparator groups. If not reported, SDs of change scores were estimated hierarchically: (1) from baseline and follow-up SDs assuming a correlation (ρ) of 0.5; (2) from reported 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for change scores; or (3) by imputation using the mean SD of change from other studies using the same outcome instrument. Sensitivity analyses used correlation assumptions (ρ) of 0.3 and 0.7. Effect sizes were expressed as MDs and SMDs (Hedges g) using the “metacont” function in the “meta” package with random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood for τ2) and Hartung-Knapp adjustment for CIs. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified with τ2 and the I2 statistic. Forest plots were generated to display study-level estimates and pooled effects.

## Results

### Study selection

As shown in our Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram (Figure 1), 5742 unique studies were screened, 141 full-text articles were reviewed, and 3 studies were added based on expert input, resulting in 53 studies. Although we searched broadly for TCT populations, only studies in HSCT recipients met inclusion criteria.

*Figure 1.: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram. Flow of information through the systematic review. Database searches identified 18 435 references (Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials [CENTRAL], CINAHL, PsycINFO, and others). Three studies were added based on expert opinion. After duplicate removal (n = 12 693), 5742 records were screened, 141 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 53 RCTs were included in the final review. Reasons for exclusion at full-text review included ineligible comparator (n = 1), ineligible intervention (n = 9), ineligible study design (n = 12), article not in English (n = 5), ineligible patient population (n = 8), ineligible outcome measurement (n = 9), not original research article (n = 37), and study protocol (n = 7).*

### Study characteristics

Table 1 summarizes the 53 included studies, grouped into 9 intervention types: cognitive behavioral (n = 5), exercise-only (n = 17), expressive helping (n = 2), mind-body/stress management (n = 7), multimodal (exercise plus another modality; n = 6); music-/art-based (n = 12), palliative care (n = 2), positive psychology (n = 1), and self-management/self-efficacy (n = 5) interventions. Exercise-only interventions were analyzed separately from multimodal programs that combined exercise with psychoeducation, mindfulness, or nutrition components, to help distinguish intervention-specific effects. Multiple reports of the same trial were collapsed into single entries, including 2 papers reporting results on a multimodal intervention31,32 and 2 papers reporting results from a single-site palliative care intervention trial.33,34 Conversely, 3 multiarm trials are presented as separate rows within respective intervention categories to reflect each active intervention type tested against a comparator group: Syrjala et al (cognitive behavioral therapy [CBT] and hypnosis),35 Syrjala et al (CBT and relaxation/imagery),36 and Jacobsen et al 2014 (exercise, stress management, and exercise plus stress management).17 After collapsing multiple reports and accounting for different arms of multiarm trials, Table 1 contains 57 rows corresponding to 53 unique RCTs. Trials included quasi-experimental (n = 2), pilot (n = 22), single-site (n = 18), and multisite (n = 11) RCTs with allogeneic HSCT recipients (n = 12), autologous HSCT recipients (n = 11), or both (n = 22); transplant type was not reported in 8 trials. Conditioning regimen was reported in 17 trials, in which patients received either myeloablative or reduced-intensity/nonmyeloablative regimens (n = 13) or myeloablative conditioning alone (n = 4). Graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis was reported in 3 trials: Amonoo et al (cyclophosphamide- and tacrolimus-based regimens),37 Dillon et al (cyclophosphamide- and cyclosporine-based regimens with methotrexate and/or mycophenolate),38 and Santa Mina et al (antithymocyte globulin–, cyclophosphamide-, and cyclosporine-based regimens with methotrexate and/or mycophenolate mofetil).39

Study sample sizes ranged from 11 to 711 participants, with mean ages of 33 to 63 years and 22% to 64% female participants across study arms. Most trials were conducted in North America (n = 30) and Europe (n = 14), with a smaller number from Asia (n = 5) and Australia (n = 4). Interventions were initiated before (n = 14), during (n = 24), or after (n = 15) HSCT hospitalization. Most were delivered in-person (n = 35), although some used home-based, remote, mixed modality, or telehealth formats.

Supplemental Table 2 lists all PRO measures by intervention type and PRO category. Across trials, PRO measures were highly heterogeneous (ie, n > 60 PRO measures) assessing diverse domains (eg, anxiety [n = 27], depression [n = 26], and other psychological and physical symptoms [n = 47], overall QOL [n = 25] and other QOL and functioning domains [n = 32], and additional intervention targets [n = 20], such as positive psychological well-being, health behaviors, self-efficacy, coping, and self-reported adherence).

### Risk of bias assessment

Figure 2 summarizes risk of bias assessments across the 5 Cochrane risk of bias 2 domains. Overall, 24 trials (45%) raised some concerns, and 29 trials (55%) were deemed at high risk of bias. Missing outcome data (Domain 3) and outcome measurement (Domain 4) represented the highest risk of bias, indicating that effect estimates from these trials should be interpreted with caution. Missing outcome data most often reflected attrition of >20% or lack of an intention-to-treat analysis, whereas outcome measurement concerns were largely due to unblinded assessors and subjective end points.

#### Cognitive behavioral interventions

Cognitive behavioral interventions lasting at least 10 sessions reduced oral pain during HSCT hospitalization and decreased distress in long-term HSCT survivors. For example, a 10-session phone-delivered CBT-based intervention in survivors 1 to 3 years after HSCT reduced symptoms of overall posttraumatic stress, depression, and general distress vs usual care up to 1 year after baseline.15 In pilot trials, cognitive behavioral skills training delivered in 6 to 7 hybrid format sessions after HSCT hospitalization was shown to be feasible and acceptable.47,52

#### Exercise (aerobic and/or strength training) interventions

Exercise programs around the time of HSCT were feasible and demonstrated promising improvements in physical function and fatigue, particularly when tailored and maintained over time. However, effects on psychological distress and QOL are limited or mixed across interventions. For example, a 3-phase, self-directed individual exercise intervention from 1 to 4 weeks before HSCT admission (prehabilitation), partly supervised by an exercise specialist during HSCT admission, and self-directed from 6 to 8 weeks after discharge (rehabilitation) reduced distress and fatigue at discharge and improved physical function and fatigue (but increased anxiety) vs an attention-matched social contact comparator group at 6 to 8 weeks after discharge.16 Conversely, a self-directed individual home-based exercise intervention (goal: 3-5 days per week for 20-30 minutes) did not improve distress or physical or mental functioning vs usual care up to 180 days after HSCT.17

#### Expressive helping (writing plus peer support) interventions

Across 2 multisite trials, a 4-session expressive helping intervention improved distress, physical symptoms, and QOL only among long-term transplant survivors with persistent symptoms but showed no benefit when delivered during the peritransplant period, even among high-symptom subgroups, suggesting that timing and targeted subgroups are critical for efficacy.98,101

#### Mind-body/stress management interventions

Intensive mind-body interventions showed feasibility and promise for reducing symptoms of anxiety, depression, and oral pain, whereas other brief or self-guided mind-body interventions showed mixed feasibility and did not improve QOL or HSCT-related symptoms vs usual care. For example, a daily 30-minute relaxation breathing and physical exercise intervention lasting 6 weeks during HSCT hospitalization reduced postintervention anxiety and depression symptoms among patients with moderate-to-severe baseline anxiety or depression,18 whereas application-based Isha Kriya practice for 12 minutes once daily from before HSCT to 30 days after HSCT did not improve overall QOL, global health, or QOL domains vs usual care, with the exception of transient improvements in bone marrow transplant–specific QOL.118

#### Multimodal interventions (exercise plus nutrition, mindfulness, or psychoeducation)

Multimodal interventions combining exercise with nutrition, mindfulness, or psychoeducation yielded mixed results, with adherence, attrition, and timing of delivery emerging as key moderators of intervention effects. Specifically, a pilot moderate-intensity supervised multimodal prehabilitation intervention showed signals of improved physical and role functioning,135 more intensive supervised inpatient interventions improved symptom burden,31,32 and outpatient or lower-intensity programs showed smaller or null effects.126

#### Music-/art-based interventions

Single music therapy sessions during HSCT hospitalization enhanced positive affect and reduced immediate fatigue, pain, and negative affect,147,149 whereas live art/music interventions allowing for patient-controlled frequency showed promise for reducing short-term symptoms of anxiety, depression, and fatigue after HSCT.140,144

#### Palliative care interventions

In single-site and multisite RCTs,33,34,165 in-person palliative care visits during HSCT hospitalization led to early improvements in depressive symptoms, overall QOL, and symptom burden with sustained reductions in posttraumatic stress symptoms up to 6 months after HSCT.

#### Positive psychology intervention

A 9-session positive psychology intervention was feasible and acceptable in allogeneic HSCT recipients, showing promising signals for psychological distress, QOL, and physical function, supporting a full-scale efficacy trial as a next step.37

#### Self-management/self-efficacy interventions

Self-management/self-efficacy interventions showed mixed, although mostly null, results, likely due to small sample sizes in pilot trials and heterogeneity of intervention content, length, and delivery. For example, an Internet-based survivorship website with self-care and mood/symptom management strategies, resources, and a patient forum and messaging platform, plus 7 biweekly sessions of telehealth problem-solving intervention showed a marginal benefit for cancer-related distress but not depressive symptoms, fatigue, or physical function vs wait-list control, 6 months after baseline.175 Furthermore, a stepped-care watchful waiting, online self-help, and optional counseling intervention showed no improvement in distress or physical functioning vs usual care up to 42 weeks after HSCT; null results in this trial were attributed, in part, to low distress and low intervention uptake.171 Finally, a pilot trial of 8-week access to a 5-module digital sexual health intervention among HSCT survivors ≥3 months after HSCT with baseline sexual dysfunction showed feasibility and promising signals for improved sexual health (ie, satisfaction with sex, interest in sex, orgasm pleasure), anxiety, depression, and overall QOL at 8 weeks after baseline.181

Overall, most interventions were deemed feasible and acceptable, with mixed effects on PROs, partly due to relatively small sample sizes for many studies and significant heterogeneity in intervention context, content, delivery, and duration. Promising reductions in psychological distress were reported for inpatient live music/art and palliative care interventions delivered during HSCT hospitalization, and cognitive behavioral, expressive helping, intensive mind-body, and brief positive psychology interventions delivered during post-HSCT recovery and survivorship. Encouraging improvements in QOL were reported for inpatient palliative care and post-HSCT positive psychology interventions, as well as among HSCT survivors with high symptom burden who engaged in an expressive helping intervention. Exercise and multimodal interventions showed primary benefits for physical functioning and symptoms.

### Exploratory meta-analyses

Of 9 intervention categories identified, only exercise and music/art interventions had at least 4 eligible RCTs reporting standardized, validated outcome measures for anxiety, depression, or overall QOL, allowing for meta-analysis based on our prespecifications.

#### Exercise intervention effects on anxiety symptoms

Four trials assessing anxiety symptoms using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) anxiety subscale54 (n = 257) were included in the MD analysis (Figure 3A).16,38,77,80 Under the primary correlation assumption (P = .5), the pooled common-effect model suggested a very small increase in anxiety in the exercise intervention group (MD, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.00-1.27), whereas the random-effects model indicated no significant effect (MD, 0.31; 95% CI, −1.83 to 2.45). Between-study heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 67.2%; τ2 = 1.11; P = .027). Sensitivity analyses varying the correlation assumption (ρ = 0.3, 0.7) yielded similar patterns, with occasional significance under common-effect models but consistently null findings under random-effects models. After adding 2 exercise trials using the GAD-7 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale)83 or the PROMIS-Anxiety (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System anxiety scale90; Figure 3B),39,92 SMDs across all 6 studies (n = 305) similarly showed no effect (SMD, 0.10; 95% CI, −0.47 to 0.66). Overall, there was no effect of exercise interventions on anxiety symptoms.

#### Exercise intervention effects on depressive symptoms

Four trials assessing depressive symptoms using the HADS-depression subscale54 (n = 257) were included in the MD analysis (Figure 3C).16,38,77,80 With ρ = 0.5, the pooled random-effects model indicated no significant effect of exercise on depressive symptoms (MD = −0.26; 95% CI: −2.83 to 2.32). Between-study heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 71.9%; τ2 = 1.80; P = .014). Sensitivity analyses with alternative correlation assumptions yielded similar nonsignificant results across both common-effect and random-effects models. After adding 2 exercise trials using the Patient Health Questionnaire-984 or PROMIS-Depression90 (Figure 3D),39,92 SMDs across all 6 studies (n = 305) also showed no overall effect (SMD, −0.02; 95% CI, −0.49 to 0.46), consistent with the null findings from the MD analysis. Overall, there was no effect of exercise interventions on depressive symptoms.

#### Exercise intervention effects on overall QOL

Ten trials assessing overall QOL using the EORTC-QLQ-C30 GHS score (European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire Core 30 Global Health Summary62; n = 505)16,39,61,63,65,75,77,92,93,96 were included (Figure 3E). With ρ = 0.5, the pooled common-effect model suggested a small improvement in overall QOL with exercise (MD, 3.64; 95% CI, 0.04-7.23), whereas the random-effects model showed a nonsignificant trend (MD, 3.64; 95% CI, −0.13 to 7.40; I2 = 0%). Sensitivity analyses with alternative correlation assumptions yielded similar estimates that remained statistically significant under the common-effect model, although random-effects models remained nonsignificant (ρ = 0.7; MD, 3.77; 95% CI, −0.12 to 7.66). After adding 2 studies using the FACT-BMT (Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy–Bone Marrow Transplant)66 total score (Figure 3F),39,38,91 SMDs across all 12 trials (n = 589) similarly showed a small, nonsignificant effect (SMD, 0.09; 95% CI, −0.08 to 0.32). Overall, exercise interventions demonstrated a trend toward improved overall QOL.

#### Music/art intervention effects on depressive symptoms

Four music/art intervention trials assessed depressive symptoms using the HADS-depression subscale (n = 86)152,155 or the Profile of Mood States–depression/dejection subscale57 (n = 142140,151; Figure 3G). SMDs across all 4 trials indicated a nonsignificant trend toward reduced depressive symptoms in common-effect models (SMD, −0.26; 95% CI, −0.52 to 0.00), reaching statistical significance under higher correlation assumptions (ρ = 0.7; SMD, −0.31; 95% CI, −0.57 to −0.05), whereas random-effects remained nonsignificant. Heterogeneity in the SMD analysis was negligible (I2 = 0%; τ2 = 0.00; P = .548). Overall, music/art interventions may confer modest reductions in depressive symptoms.

## Discussion

To our knowledge, this systematic review and meta-analysis is among the first to examine RCTs of supportive care interventions and their effects on PROs in patients with hematologic malignancies undergoing HSCT within the past decade. Notably, although we searched broadly for TCT studies, the search yielded only interventions for the HSCT population, suggesting that RCTs of supportive care intervention effects on PROs among patients receiving cellular therapies (eg, CAR T-cell therapy) have not yet been published. Our review highlights the substantial heterogeneity in supportive care intervention content, delivery, duration, and context across the HSCT trajectory, from prehabilitation to rehabilitation. Most interventions were feasible and acceptable, with several intervention approaches (eg, inpatient palliative care and live music/art interventions, as well as post-HSCT–delivered cognitive behavioral, expressive helping, mind-body, and positive psychology interventions) showing promise for reducing psychological distress (eg, symptoms of anxiety, depression, posttraumatic stress). Despite 3 decades of growing interest in psychosocial and rehabilitative interventions for transplant recipients, intervention effects were not consistent across trials. This heterogeneity in intervention content and delivery was anticipated given the broad conceptualization of supportive care and reflects diverse supportive care models across HSCT settings.

Many of the included trials were designed as pilot trials to assess intervention feasibility and acceptability, rather than single-site or multisite trials powered to assess intervention effects on PROs. This aligns with intervention development frameworks (eg, Obesity Related Behavioral Intervention Trials [ORBIT], National Institutes of Health [NIH] Stage Model),183,184 which emphasize rigorous feasibility testing before full-scale efficacy trials. However, the high proportion of feasibility studies underscores the emerging nature of this field.185 Larger, multisite RCTs are needed to determine intervention effects on PROs and definitively establish the efficacy of existing interventions. Although many interventions demonstrated feasibility and acceptability, relatively few progressed to larger efficacy trials. This limited progression may reflect barriers common in supportive care research, including funding constraints, resource-intensive protocols, attrition of multidisciplinary teams between feasibility and implementation phases, and potential publication bias that obscures negative or null findings.

Patients undergoing HSCT experience significant physical and psychological symptoms throughout the HSCT trajectory.186 However, of the trials we included, very few interventions (eg, palliative care and exercise interventions) specifically targeted physical and psychological symptoms,6,165 highlighting the need for further research on supportive care trials in this important area.187 Considering the interrelationship between physical and psychological outcomes in HSCT,188 the potential benefits of behavioral interventions to improve physical and psychological symptoms in seriously ill populations,189 and the limited number of multimodal interventions currently available, future trials should assess multimodal interventions that concurrently address physical and psychological symptoms and health behaviors. Comparative effectiveness studies examining intervention effects on physical and psychological symptoms are also needed to determine which specific interventions are most effective for specific symptom profiles.

Many barriers continue to limit patient access to timely supportive care interventions and should be addressed. First, aside from 1 palliative care intervention trial,165 few multisite RCTs have been conducted and/or demonstrated efficacy, limiting dissemination and implementation in clinical practice.190 Second, despite evidence that phone-delivered supportive care is feasible and effective in general oncology populations,191 most interventions were delivered in-person, likely reflecting prolonged hospitalizations and frequent routine follow-up care among HSCT recipients.192 Data on supportive care interventions targeting patients undergoing outpatient HSCT remain limited. Third, more scalable models are needed, as most interventions required in-person delivery by specialist clinicians (eg, palliative care clinicians, mental health providers, physiotherapists), who are already scarce even at major academic transplant centers.193,194 Future studies should evaluate cost or health care system outcomes, critical considerations for determining the resources (beyond human personnel) needed to implement supportive care interventions,195 and adapt interventions for languages other than English to ensure accessibility for non-English–speaking patients, who may already face disparities in psychosocial care in the United States.196 Table 3 summarizes recommendations for future trials to ensure methodologic rigor and enhance potential for widespread adoption of supportive care interventions that are shown to be efficacious.

Our exploratory meta-analyses generally mirrored the qualitative synthesis: exercise interventions showed a trend toward improvements in QOL but no impact on psychological distress, consistent with previous reviews, which found benefits for QOL but no effects on distress.197,198 The broader literature suggests that exercise may confer benefits through reductions in fatigue and sleep disturbance as well as improved physical functioning.197,199, 200, 201, 202, 203 Notably, previous meta-analyses grouped exercise and multimodal interventions together under a single “exercise” category, whereas in this review we analyzed exercise-only trials separately and synthesized multimodal programs qualitatively. This distinction may partly explain variability in observed effect sizes and highlights the need for clearer categorization in future studies. Several reviews further emphasize the importance of timing, with pretransplant initiation generally associated with greater benefits than posttransplant delivery.197, 198, 199 Music/art interventions demonstrated small benefits for mood and affect, likely reflecting acute mood improvements because they were delivered in-person during hospitalization, typically in single sessions, with outcomes measured immediately afterward. This is consistent with previous literature showing music intervention to reduce short-term depressive symptoms in HSCT.204 Future studies should assess sustainability beyond the inpatient setting. Given the substantial heterogeneity in intervention content, timing, and patient populations across the included studies, pooled estimates of exploratory meta-analyses should be interpreted with caution and viewed as exploratory signals to guide future hypothesis-driven research rather than definitive efficacy estimates. Importantly, a lack of sufficient evidence in certain intervention categories should not be interpreted as evidence of no effect but rather reflects the limited number of comparable RCTs available for quantitative synthesis.

Several study limitations warrant consideration. Although we only included RCTs, many trials had methodological concerns (eg, suboptimal randomization or blinding), and some trials were not prospectively registered, limiting assessments of study rigor. Exclusion of conference abstracts may have excluded emerging pilot data. Most studies were pilot trials with small sample sizes, limiting statistical power to detect differential effects of interventions vs comparator conditions and necessitating caution in interpreting pooled estimates as exploratory. Moreover, the high risk of publication bias in more than half of included studies, primarily due to missing outcome data and outcome measurement concerns, further limits confidence in observed intervention effects, particularly for intervention categories supported primarily by pilot or single-site studies. Overall, the predominance of pilot work and limited progression to full-scale efficacy testing constrains the strength of the current evidence base. Furthermore, interventions varied in timing, content, duration, and delivery, and different PROs were used at varying time points. Spiritual care interventions fall within our definition of supportive care and were included within our search strategy, but no spiritual care studies ultimately met inclusion criteria (eg, study design, patient population), potentially limiting generalizability across the full spectrum of supportive care modalities. Limited data on sociodemographic factors and predominantly ethnic majority participants limit generalizability to ethnic minority populations. Finally, several included trials enrolled mixed HSCT recipient populations (eg, malignant and nonmalignant disease) with unequal representation of transplantation type (ie, autologous vs allogeneic) and limited data on clinical factors that have potential to affect outcomes (eg, conditioning regimen, graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis), warranting caution when interpreting HSCT-specific effects.

After 3 decades, RCTs have largely demonstrated feasibility of supportive care interventions in patients undergoing HSCT for hematologic malignancies, whereas none have been tested in patients undergoing cellular therapies (eg, CAR T-cell therapy) and evidence of efficacy for improving PROs remains limited. Larger, rigorously designed, multisite trials using standardized PRO measures are needed to establish efficacy and inform implementation of supportive care interventions in routine clinical care.
